concerns.message: Acceptance item 4 needs committed golden-trace fixtures, but it doesn't say what format they take or how the tests load them, and the obvious routes all fail checks controlled by files outside the owned paths. (1) `packages/simulation/tsconfig.json` has `types: []`, and neither it nor `tsconfig.base.json` sets `resolveJsonModule`. So `import traces from "./golden.json"` fails `npm run typecheck` (TS2732). `readFileSync` fails too: there are no Node typings. (2) `tests/unit/purity.test.ts` scans every `.ts` file under `packages/simulation/src`, test files included, and rejects `node:fs` imports. Loading a fixture from disk in a duel test therefore fails `test:unit`. (3) Writing the traces needs `fs` as well, so a recorder can't live in the owned paths either (`scripts/` isn't owned). (4) Dumping the full traces as a TypeScript array of objects would make a file of roughly 7–10 MB (3 × 3,600 frames × two fighters × about 17 fields plus events). `tsc` is known to be very slow or run out of memory on literals that large. The typecheck check has a 300 s limit. Also, `tsconfig.build.json` excludes only `*.test.ts`, so any such file would be compiled into `dist`.
concerns.consequence: The worker's first natural approach fails typecheck or the purity test. The Stop rule says "a check can pass only by changing a path outside the owned paths", so the worker may reasonably report `blocked`, or spend the time budget fighting the checks. Either way the one item that proves backward compatibility stalls. Settle it in one sentence first. The fixtures are a generated `.ts` module in `packages/simulation/src/duel`. It holds strings: per-frame canonical text or hashes of the projected legacy fields, events, phase and result, plus optional full checkpoints every N frames. A throwaway recorder run from outside the repo writes it at the base commit, and the test loads it with a plain import.

concerns.message: With only optional `projectile?`, `zone?` and `cancel?` sub-objects, the move data has nothing that says what a move is meant to do. First, the feint has neither `projectile` nor `zone`, so `strikesWithHitbox` would have to treat `cancel` as meaning "doesn't strike". That mixes up two separate properties: a later cancellable strike would silently stop hitting. Second, the feint is still `kind: "strike"`. It must carry unused `damage` (the schema requires it to be positive), `hitstun` and `blockstun`, and they must satisfy the blockstun = active + recovery + advantage rule. Third, acceptance item 1's invalid-kit case, "a projectile move without projectile data is refused", can't be written at all: under optional sub-objects such a move is just a valid strike.
concerns.consequence: The worker either makes up a discriminator partway through the work or ties the check to particular kit slots (for example, ember.special1 must have a projectile), which puts kit semantics into the schema. The feint's unused `damage` field could also end up in the "Smoke deals less damage" comparison. Fix: add one explicit optional field to each move, for example `effect: "strike" | "projectile" | "zone" | "feint"` (default `strike`), and base both the schema check and `strikesWithHitbox` on it.

concerns.message: Acceptance item 2 says the flare hits "at a height where the universal anti-air misses". With the current data there is no such height. The anti-air's hitbox spans y = 48–144 px. The airborne hurtbox spans y to y+80, and the jump's apex is y = 105 px (jumpVelocity 160, gravity 8). The two always overlap vertically. The anti-air misses only on range: its reach is about 66 px (hitbox 0–48 px plus the 18 px half-width of the airborne hurtbox). The design section says "heights and ranges"; the acceptance item says only "height".
concerns.consequence: A worker who reads the acceptance literally can't write the test. They might change the anti-air data instead, which breaks the golden traces and the requirement that normals stay the same. Reword the item as "at a range where the anti-air misses".

concerns.message: "Smoke's damage per hit is lower than the Duelist's equivalents" is empty under the settled design. The feint and the screen deal no damage, and normals and the throw are shared. So every Smoke hit does exactly what the Duelist's equivalent does. The Smoke-vulnerability exchange in item 5 ("low direct damage") has the same problem.
concerns.consequence: The worker either writes a test that proves nothing (0 < 130, or comparing the feint's unused `damage` field) or adds per-kit damage scaling to normals. Scaling would contradict §9's "core normals remain". State the check in terms of exchanges instead: for example, Smoke's best punish on a whiffed flare, or its best damage after a feint, is less than the Duelist's advancing-thrust punish in the same situation.

concerns.message: The design says "each frame checks the whole path the bolt moved" but doesn't say how. The literal reading is to test whether the two bolts' swept boxes (start-to-end paths) overlap. That gives false "meets" for two bolts travelling the same way, which a cross-up makes possible: two same-speed bolts a few pixels apart never touch, but their swept boxes overlap. The same false positives can appear between a bolt's path and a hurtbox that is moving away from it.
concerns.consequence: In Ember-vs-Ember and cross-up exchanges, bolts that never touched destroy each other. Worse, the property tests don't catch it, because the invariants still hold. Specify the test in terms of relative motion: the boxes overlap at some point during the frame, computed from 1-D integer interval arithmetic on relative velocity.

concerns.message: The golden duels use random inputs over 3,600 frames. A random-mashing Duelist mirror probably ends in a KO well before 3,600 frames. Once `result` is set, the step only advances `frame`, so the rest of the trace tests nothing. Uniform random bits also rarely produce throw escapes, throw clashes, guard breaks or the throw-chord path.
concerns.consequence: The "Duelist mirror unchanged" proof covers fewer step paths than its size suggests. A regression in a rarely taken branch, for example throw-escape event order after the bolt-resolution rewrite, passes unnoticed. Fix: bias the inputs to keep duels alive, or restart from a new seed when a result appears, and record branch coverage in `docs/fruit-kits.md`.

simpler_alternative: Keep the settled kit design, but make the golden-trace proof and the move model simpler. (a) Golden fixtures: a generated TypeScript module exporting, for each of the three seeds, an array of per-frame hashes of the projected legacy fields (every existing FighterState field, events, phase, result), plus a full JSON-string checkpoint every 300 frames for diagnosis. That's about 200 KB instead of about 10 MB. It loads with a plain import, so it needs no `fs`, no JSON imports and no tsconfig change. A recorder script outside the repo writes it at the base commit, before the step is touched. (b) Move model: replace the implied roles of the optional sub-objects with one explicit `effect` field (strike | projectile | zone | feint, default strike). `strikesWithHitbox` becomes `effect === \"strike\"`, the schema requires `projectile` exactly when `effect === \"projectile\"` (the same for zone), and the \"projectile move without projectile data\" refusal becomes a one-line check.
cheap_experiment: This takes about 10 minutes in a scratch copy of the base commit, before the worker starts. Add three throwaway files under `packages/simulation/src/duel`: (1) a test that imports a small `.json` file; (2) a test that imports `readFileSync` from `node:fs`; (3) a generated `.ts` module holding one full 3,600-frame Duelist-mirror trace as an object literal, and a second one holding the same trace as an array of hash strings. Run `npm run typecheck` and `npx vitest run --project unit tests/unit/purity.test.ts`, and time `tsc -p packages/simulation/tsconfig.json` for each. The expected result is that (1) and (2) fail and the hash-string module compiles in seconds. If it does, the fixture format in the P1 is settled with evidence. Log in the same run how many frames each seeded random duel lasts before `result` is set, to check the coverage concern.
